title: Why Allowing Students To Turn In Work Anytime Is A Bad Idea me-is-a-bad-idea/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin pushes back against a trend among educational leaders of eliminating deadlines in the name of equity, arguing the practice does real harm. He cites four reasons: deadlines motivate effort and performance while their absence breeds apathy and procrastination; compounding, undone work becomes discouraging and is often abandoned rather than completed; students who fall behind lose the prerequisite skills needed for future learning; and meeting deadlines teaches time-management and responsibility that serve students for life. He is skeptical of the rationale offered for removing deadlines, arguing that framing it as 'standards-based grading' actually strips out standards while shielding administrators from criticism. He does carve out a caveat for students with excused absences or genuine special circumstances, for whom deadlines should be adjusted individually rather than eliminated for everyone.
points: Deadlines are proven to improve motivation, effort, and performance; removing them breeds apathy and procrastination.
Allowing work to pile up indefinitely creates discouragement that often leads students to abandon it entirely.
Students who fall behind lack the prerequisite skills for more advanced learning, making success nearly impossible.
Meeting deadlines trains transferable life skills like time-management, punctuality, and responsibility.
Deadlines should still be adjusted individually for students with excused absences or genuine special circumstances.
quotes: There is a growing sentiment among educational leaders that students should be able to turn in work anytime without penalty, even weeks after the due date.
Mountains of research confirm what your instincts are probably already telling you: Deadlines improve motivation , produce greater effort, and result in better performance.
Seeing work pile up causes immense stress. It creates discouragement and hopelessness as the task becomes more daunting as time goes on.
The discipline needed to meet deadlines trains students in critical life and success skills like time-management, punctuality, responsibility , and integrity.
The powers that be are hiding a removal of standards by calling them standards . They’re also stating that deadlines are discriminatory against certain groups of students.
Note: Of course, if students have excused absences, connectivity issues, special circumstances, etc., then teachers should adjust deadlines accordingly.
